c.v: Explain, in writing and without looking anything up, the difference between localisation and SLAM: what each is given, what each produces, and when you would run one rather than the other. Then say which of the two the bench's robot is doing today and why that was the right choice. Take 10 minutes.

Localisation is given a map and asked where the robot is in it. The map is fixed, the robot's pose is the unknown, and the answer is produced by comparing what the sensors see now with what the map says should be visible from each candidate pose. SLAM, simultaneous localisation and mapping, is given no map and asked for both at once: where the robot is and what the world looks like. It is the harder problem because the two unknowns depend on each other, and the reason it works at all is that revisiting a place you have seen before constrains both, which is what loop closure is.

You run localisation when a map exists and the world matches it closely enough: a warehouse, a factory floor, a building you surveyed last month. You run SLAM when it does not, which is the first visit to a site, a space that has been rearranged, or a robot that is expected to work somewhere nobody has surveyed. SLAM is also what you run once to produce the map that localisation then uses for a year.
The bench's robot is doing neither, and that is the answer worth giving. It has odometry from the wheels and nothing that corrects it: no map, no scan matching, no

frame being published by anything. Its pose is dead reckoning, which drifts, and the scenarios it runs are short enough and judged on distances small enough that the drift does not reach the tolerances. That was the right choice because the bench's claims are about the supervisor and the stopping behaviour, and adding a localiser would add a component whose failures would show up inside every one of those claims without testing any of them.

You pass if localisation is given a map and SLAM is not, both outputs are named, and the choice rule mentions whether a map exists. Adding the bench's answer is worth full marks on its own. Describing SLAM as "localisation but better" is a fail: it is a different problem with a different failure mode, and running it where a map already exists throws away the one thing you were sure of.
Navigation is the layer that turns "go to that pose" into velocity commands, and in ROS 2 the standard implementation is Nav2, a set of separate nodes rather than one program.

The problem it solves has four parts, and Nav2 keeps them apart on purpose. Knowing where you are: a localiser matches sensor readings against a stored map, or SLAM builds the map as it goes. Knowing what is around you: a costmap turns the map and the live sensor data into a grid where each cell carries a cost, with obstacles inflated by roughly the robot's radius so a planner can treat the robot as a point. Deciding where to go: a global planner searches that grid for a path to the goal. Following it: a local controller produces velocities that track the path while avoiding what the planner did not know about.

The mechanism holding them together is a behaviour tree. A navigator node runs a tree whose leaves call the planner and the controller as actions, and whose branches decide what to do when one of them fails: try again, spin in place, back up, wait, or give up and report. That is where recovery lives, and it is the part that makes the difference between a robot that stops when it is confused and one that gets itself out.

What it costs is a long list of assumptions, most of which a real building breaks. The localiser assumes the map still matches the building and that it was given a roughly correct starting pose. The costmap assumes the sensor data arrives in the right frame and fresh, so a stale transform quietly becomes an obstacle in the wrong place. The controller assumes the path it was handed is drivable by this robot.

Where you meet it is debugging, and the useful skill is knowing which of the four parts to look at. A robot that plans a path through a wall has a costmap problem; one that plans correctly and drives into things has a controller or a sensor problem; one that is confidently in the wrong room has a localisation problem, and no amount of planner tuning will help.

c.v: Nav2 is not one program. It is about a dozen nodes that each do one job, and the first useful thing to know is which is which, because a fault always belongs to one of them. The names below and the default plugins come from
on the jazzy branch, which is the file every real deployment starts from.

. AMCL stands for adaptive Monte Carlo localisation, and the mechanism is a particle filter: a few thousand candidate poses, each scored by how well a laser scan taken from that pose would match the stored map, resampled so that good candidates multiply and bad ones die out. It is given a map and an initial pose, and it publishes the

transform, which is the correction between where odometry thinks the robot is and where the map says it is. That transform is the whole output, and the frames topic already covered why it is published as a correction to odometry rather than as a pose.

Three assumptions come with it. The map has to still be the building: move the shelves and the scan stops matching. The initial pose has to be roughly right, because a particle filter is a local method and will happily converge on a wrong corridor that looks like the right one. And the odometry has to be reasonable, because the filter uses it to move the particles between scans.
is the other branch, and in Jazzy the usual package is

, which lives outside Nav2. It solves the harder problem of building the map while localising in it, and the thing to know for an interview is what makes it work: loop closure. When the robot recognises a place it has been before, that recognition is a constraint between two parts of the trajectory, and a graph optimisation adjusts everything between them to make the two agree. Without loop closure a SLAM map is odometry with scans stapled to it, and it bends.

, and there are two of them. The global costmap covers the whole map, updates slowly, and is what the planner searches; the default sets it to 1 Hz. The local costmap is a small rolling window around the robot, updates fast, and is what the controller avoids things with; the default is 5 Hz with a 2 Hz publish. Each is built from layers applied in order, and the defaults differ between the two: the global one uses a static layer from the map, an obstacle layer from the laser and an inflation layer, and the local one uses a voxel layer and an inflation layer.

The inflation layer is the one worth understanding, because it is where most tuning happens. It grows every obstacle by a decaying cost field, so a cell near a wall is expensive rather than forbidden. That does two things: it lets the planner treat the robot as a point, because the robot's radius has already been added to the obstacles, and it makes paths prefer the middle of a corridor without anyone writing a rule that says so. Set the inflation radius smaller than the robot and the planner will plan paths the robot cannot drive; set it much larger and it will refuse to plan through doors.
, which loads a planner plugin; the default is
, a grid search over the global costmap. Alternatives in the same repository include
, which can respect a car-like robot's turning radius, and

. The planner's contract is narrow and worth stating: it takes a start and a goal pose and returns a path, it does not know how fast the robot goes, and it assumes the robot can follow any path it produces.
The rate it runs at is a question worth getting right, because the obvious answer is wrong. There is a parameter called
, set to 20.0 in the defaults, and it does not schedule anything: the only code that reads it turns it into
and uses that to warn when one planning call took longer than it (
). It is an overrun warning threshold, not a rate. What actually decides how often the planner runs is the behaviour tree, which wraps the call to
, and says so in its own header comment: this tree replans the global path periodically at 1 Hz (

). So the path is recomputed once a second while the controller runs at twenty, which makes a path a current opinion rather than a commitment, and makes the local costmap and the controller responsible for everything that happens in between.
, which loads a controller plugin and runs it at 20 Hz by default. Jazzy's default is
, a sampling method that rolls out many candidate velocity sequences, scores them against the path, the costmap and its own criteria, and takes a weighted average. The repository also carries
, which follows the path geometrically and slows down for curvature and obstacles, and

, which turns to face the path before handing over. Alongside the controller run a progress checker, which fails the action when the robot has not moved far enough in a given time, and a goal checker, which decides when close enough is arrived.

. The navigator runs a behaviour tree, and the tree is where the sequencing lives: compute a path, follow it, and on failure run a recovery and try again. The default recoveries are spin, back up, drive on heading, assisted teleop and wait. A behaviour tree is worth a sentence of explanation because the name is opaque: it is a tree of nodes that each return success, failure or running, with control nodes that sequence their children or fall back to the next one when a child fails, so the whole policy is data in an XML file rather than code. Changing when the robot backs up is an edit to that file.
Three more nodes complete the picture.
brings the others up in a fixed order using the lifecycle transitions the executors topic described, so nothing starts planning before the map server has a map.
limits the acceleration of the commands before they reach the base, and

is a separate, deliberately simple node that watches raw sensor data and stops the robot when something is too close, independent of everything above it. That last one is the same idea as the bench's supervisor, arrived at by the same reasoning: the component that stops the robot should not be the component that might be confused.
The interfaces between all of this are actions, which the services and actions topic covered.
are what an application calls. Inside, the tree calls
on the controller. Because they are actions, every one of them can report progress and be cancelled, which is what makes a navigation stack interruptible.
That leaves the question this page exists to answer, which is what to look at when it misbehaves. Work down the list in order. Is the robot where it thinks it is? Compare the

transform with reality, and if it is wrong nothing downstream can be right. Does the costmap show what is actually there? Look at it in RViz, because a costmap with an obstacle that is not there and a costmap missing one that is both produce confident wrong plans. Is the path sensible? A path through a wall is a costmap or an inflation problem, not a planner bug. Is the robot following the path? If the path is good and the motion is not, the controller, the velocity smoother or the base is where to look. Four questions, in that order, and each one eliminates everything below it.

Write five to eight lines from memory, and keep them as the proof for this topic. Give the difference between localisation and SLAM in terms of what each is given and produces, and name the mechanism each relies on. Name the four parts of a navigation stack and the Nav2 node that provides each. Say what a costmap is, what the inflation layer does and what goes wrong when its radius is too small or too large. Give the two costmaps and roughly how often each updates. Say where recovery lives and name three recoveries. Finish with the four debugging questions in the order you would ask them.
